name: Bell / Buzzer
tagline: A solenoid that hammers a gong: the load at the far end of the doorbell circuit.
terminals: Two terminals on a simple AC bell or buzzer
Earth where the bell has a metal case
parts: Gong — the metal dome or plate that makes the sound
Striker — the arm that hits it
Solenoid coil — pulls the armature in when energised
Contacts — break the circuit so the striker springs back and strikes again
Bell transformer — steps 230 V down to 8–12 V
safety: Bell circuits usually run at extra-low voltage, but the transformer feeding them is mains. It must be mounted where it cannot be touched accidentally, be short-circuit protected, and be isolated before any work. A bell that hums without ringing usually has a broken striker or a seized armature, not an electrical fault.

points.label: Gong
points.detail: The tuned metal dome. Its size and fixing decide the note: tighten it against the case and it deadens, hold it on a resilient mounting and it rings.

points.label: Solenoid coil
points.detail: Energise it and the magnetic field pulls the armature in; the same movement opens a contact, the field collapses, and the spring drives it back. That cycle repeats for as long as the button is held, which is why a bell rattles rather than sounding one note.

points.label: Striker
points.detail: The arm and its clapper. It must just reach the gong: too far and the coil cannot pull it in, too close and it jams against the dome and only buzzes.

points.label: Terminals
points.detail: Two terminals on an AC bell or buzzer; polarity only matters on a DC unit with electronics in it. The bell draws a fraction of an amp, but the inrush of the coil is many times that, which is worth remembering if you ever switch it with a relay.

points.label: Base and mounting
points.detail: Fix the base to something solid — a bell screwed to a hollow door frame sounds like it. The mounting screws also carry the case earth on metal-bodied units.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of an electric bell showing the solenoid coil, armature and striker, gong, self-interrupting contacts and return spring

cutawayPoints.label: Solenoid coil
cutawayPoints.detail: Fed from the bell transformer at 8–12 V, not from the mains. Energised, it pulls the armature in to strike the gong — and because it is a coil it keeps drawing current only while the striker is moving, which is what makes the interrupting contact essential.

cutawayPoints.label: Armature and striker
cutawayPoints.detail: A spring-steel arm carrying the striker, hinged so the coil pull swings it at the gong. Its travel sets how hard the gong is hit, so a striker set too close buzzes weakly and one set too far never reaches it.

cutawayPoints.label: Gong
cutawayPoints.detail: The tuned metal dome that turns the strike into a sound. It is the resonator, not the mechanism: a gong screwed down hard against its mounting, or touching the case, is muffled instead of ringing — the usual reason a bell sounds like a buzzer.

cutawayPoints.label: Self-interrupting contacts
cutawayPoints.detail: The contacts that make it a bell rather than a solenoid: as the armature arrives, they open, the coil de-energises, the striker springs back, they close again and it strikes once more. That cycle repeating several times a second is the buzz you hear.

cutawayPoints.label: Return spring
cutawayPoints.detail: Pulls the striker back off the gong so it can strike again, and holds the contacts closed when the bell is at rest. It also sets the rest position, so a weak spring leaves the striker resting on the gong and the bell silent.

cutawayPoints.label: Terminals
cutawayPoints.detail: Two screws fed at SELV from the bell transformer, which is why the cable to a bell is not treated like a lighting circuit and why the transformer itself is the part that fails when a bell goes quiet — check for voltage here before condemning the bell.
